chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ibrahim ibn Imran al-Shaybani, from Yunus ibn Ibrahim, from Yahya ibn Ash'ath al-Kinani, from Mus'ab ibn Yazid al-Ansari, who said:
The Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), appointed me over four districts of Madain: Bahqubadhat, Bahrsir, Nahr Juyar, and Nahr al-Malik.

He ordered me to impose on every jarib of thick-crop land one dirham and a half, on every jarib of medium-crop land one dirham, on every jarib of thin-crop land two-thirds of a dirham, on every jarib of vineyard ten dirhams, on every jarib of palm trees ten dirhams, and on every jarib of orchards that combine palms and trees ten dirhams.
He ordered me to exempt every stray palm tree outside the villages for travelers and wayfarers, and not to take anything from it.

He ordered me to impose on the dehqans (landed gentry) who ride bareds and wear gold signet rings, on every man of them forty-eight dirhams; on their middle class and merchants, on every man twenty-four dirhams; and on their lower class and poor, on every person twelve dirhams.
He said: So I collected it, eighteen million dirhams in one year.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: Therefore, what this report contains of mentioning something of the jizyah fixed from every person is not inconsistent with what we mentioned, that it is up to the Imam to take from them according to what he sees fit at the time, because it is not impossible that the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) saw it as expedient to impose on every man of them the mentioned amount in that year, and if the expediency changed to increase or decrease, he would also change it. And it would only be inconsistent if he imposed that on them and said, 'This is their ruling, and they shall not be increased or decreased from it in all circumstances,' and that is not in the report.
ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali determine land and poll tax rates in Madain?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this narration highlights Imam Ali’s administrative pragmatism in managing the tax districts of Madain, where he tailored levies to crop quality and social stratification. The accompanying commentary by al-Tusi clarifies that these rates were not immutable divine laws but flexible fiscal policies subject to change based on the Imam’s assessment of public interest (maslahah). This underscores the Shia jurisprudential view that the Imam possesses the authority to adjust financial obligations dynamically to serve the community's needs.
